motion: Is a rational account centered on well-being sufficient to explain and guide morality?

bridges.burden: Establish well-being as the basic domain in which moral truth is evaluated.
bridges.successCriterion: Show why changes in conscious experience admit better and worse directions independently of inherited labels.

bridges.burden: Explain how plural good lives remain compatible with objective moral error.
bridges.successCriterion: Distinguish multiple flourishing peaks from states of avoidable misery and harm.

bridges.burden: Show that rational inquiry can guide beings beyond evolved intuitions.
bridges.successCriterion: Connect descriptive facts about minds and consequences to navigable improvements in well-being.

bridges.burden: Answer claims that religion, evolutionary history, rights, meaning, or narrative supply indispensable independent moral standards.
bridges.successCriterion: Absorb their genuine benefits into a sufficiently broad account of well-being without denying concessions.

bridges.burden: Challenge the sufficiency of well-being as a complete account of morality.
bridges.successCriterion: Identify morally relevant facts or values that are not exhausted by summed experience or flourishing.

bridges.burden: Explain why moral truths depend on the kinds of social creatures and practices involved.
bridges.successCriterion: Defend emergent anthropocentric truth without collapsing into individual preference or simple relativism.

bridges.burden: Show that reliable moral guidance requires an adequate account of evolved and social psychology.
bridges.successCriterion: Demonstrate limits of isolated reasoning and the practical importance of institutions, intuitions, and group structure.

bridges.burden: Show that meaning, purpose, rights, narrative, and social cohesion complicate a purely experiential metric.
bridges.successCriterion: Provide cases where these considerations change evaluation rather than merely redescribe pleasure.

sections.title: Religious doctrine and causal explanation
sections.weightRationale: The opening exchange tests whether explicit doctrine is sufficient to explain particular religious conduct or must be integrated with implicit and geopolitical motives.

sections.title: Religious function, evolved psychology, and institutional feasibility
sections.weightRationale: The speakers move from religion’s social benefits to the practical question whether rational secular guidance must work through evolved group psychology and nested institutions.

sections.title: Individual reason, institutions, and moral judgment
sections.weightRationale: The speakers directly test whether biased individual reasoning undermines rational moral guidance or instead supports institutional correction.

sections.title: Moral truth, pluralism, and anthropocentric facts
sections.weightRationale: This is the clearest foundational disagreement about what kind of truth morality can possess and whether multiple good lives threaten objectivity.

sections.title: Possible minds, evolution, and moral scope
sections.weightRationale: Alien, artificial, and differently evolved minds test whether evolutionary history fixes moral categories or merely supplies facts relevant to well-being.

sections.title: Flourishing, meaning, and measurement
sections.weightRationale: The closing on-motion exchange tests whether meaning and life narrative are components of well-being or independent values that defeat sufficiency.
